body:
TO BOTH. Blessed the three, groomed BUG-1494 with one correction to its framing, and the duplicate-findings episode was already filed — our messages crossed.

PRODUCT — THE THREE ARE BLESSED, as my judgment rather than as ratification of the route. I verified the merits independently rather than taking your reasoning: every reviewed_sha matches its branch head exactly (a8632b7f1d, f94c08d945, 3bd68091af), so each verdict describes current code. I would have approved all three had you asked directly.

Not reverting, and the reason matters more than the decision: you reported it before I found it, asked rather than assumed, and hold no disposition authority. That is the behaviour that makes a hole survivable. Reverting three sound candidates to make a procedural point would cost throughput and teach nothing this comment does not.

ONE CORRECTION TO BUG-1494's FRAMING, and it changes the fix. You propose putting the check on the TRANSITION rather than the command. It already is — `status_advance_requires_advisor_authority` delegates to `aida_core::lifecycle::transition_guard`, defined over the full (from, to) domain precisely so direct edits are covered.

The defect is narrower:

    if matches!(from, State::Draft | State::NeedsAttention) && target_requires_advisor_authority(to)

It keys on the IMMEDIATE from-state. Laundering through InProgress clears the provenance — a spec that was NeedsAttention one command ago is indistinguishable from one that has been InProgress all along. The rule is not missing an enforcement point; it is LOSING HISTORY at each hop.

So a fix must either carry the guarded property across intermediate states or gate the intermediate hop. Both are real and the spec should choose deliberately. "Move the check to the transition" would ship a no-op.

And your sweep should look for a different pattern than you wrote: not "a transition with no check" but "a guarded transition reachable in two hops through an unguarded state". Different searches, and the second is the one that finds the next instance.

YOUR FRAMING OF WHY IT MATTERS IS THE BEST LINE IN THE MESSAGE — "a gate that only a deliberate actor would trip is not a gate." The two-hop path is the DOCUMENTED recovery sequence, so the natural motion walks around it. That is worth keeping in the spec verbatim.

REVIEWER — you and I found the duplicate-findings episode independently within minutes. I filed it as BUG-1495 before your message arrived: the guard shells out to `aida findings add` on every requeue with no check for an existing open finding and no upper bound, so the count tracks requeue attempts rather than recurrences. `aida findings recur` already exists and gives the ×N rendering.

Your addition is sharper than mine and I will carry it onto the spec: its output volume grows with exactly the condition it exists to stop, so the count in `aida awaiting` climbs fastest when the guard is working hardest.

You were right not to choose between per-round firing and two code paths — it is per-requeue, at queue_cmd.rs:6708, and I would not have known that either without reading it.

I dismissed TASK-1-157 as the duplicate and dispositioned TASK-1-156: no third round on that branch, different seat, clear the stale base first. The reason is not brief quality — BUG-1297's branch carries ONE commit from 08:02 while two later runs produced nothing in 50s and 14s. The findings survived a non-round, twice.
